# Judge a specification by whether its rules are generated by a compact schema and only a few are ever live, not by how many rules it has

**Lesson:** The description Edmonds gives of the matching problem contains one constraint for every odd-sized subset of vertices, which is astronomically many for any graph worth talking about, and he says plainly that the count does not matter and the combinatorial structure does. That claim inverts the usual instinct. What makes a description workable is not its cardinality but two other properties: the whole family is generated by a single stated schema, so writing it down and reasoning about all of it costs no more than reasoning about the schema; and at any moment only a small number of members are actually doing work, bounded by something like the size of the input rather than the size of the family. He makes the second property concrete by noting that although the dual vector nominally has an enormous number of components, any vector he will ever handle has at most as many nonzero components as there are edges. The huge object is never materialized.

The same shape recurs in the branching paper, whose inequality family again ranges over all subsets of nodes and again is generated by one rule with one parameter. In both cases the schema is what gets reasoned about, the instantiations are what get touched, and the gap between the two is where the tractability lives. This is why a large rule space is not automatically a design smell: an exponential family with a one-line generator and a sparse active set is easier to hold in your head, and easier to prove things about, than a few dozen hand-written special cases with no common form. The primitive count that matters is the number of independent constructs the schema needs, not the number of objects the schema denotes.

Applied outside combinatorics, this is a test to run on any configuration language, validation layer, permission model, or type system. Are the rules instances of a stated pattern, or a list someone appends to? Can you bound how many are relevant to a single decision, or must the implementation scan all of them? A rule set that fails both tests is a maintenance problem no matter how short it currently is, because every new case is a new independent thing to remember. A rule set that passes both can grow without bound and stay comprehensible, and it can be implemented by generating the relevant members on demand rather than storing them.

**Source:** [Maximum Matching and a Polyhedron with 0,1-Vertices](../works/maximum-matching-and-a-polyhedron-with-0-1-vertices.md) — the introductory claim about relevant inequality counts versus their structure, the observation that only a good characterization of the bounding family matters rather than a minimal one, and the remark bounding the nonzero components of any dual vector actually handled. Also [Optimum Branchings](../works/optimum-branchings.md), whose inequality system is likewise a single schema quantified over all subsets of nodes, with a dual variable introduced per member and only a handful ever nonzero.
